body:
The young Buffett was a hustler before he was an investor. Newspaper routes, golf balls and pinball machines produced about **$9,800 in savings** by the time he finished school ([Saber Capital](https://sabercapitalmgt.com/buffetts-early-investments/)). His research edge was volume. He reportedly went through about **20,000 pages of Moody's manuals, twice**, and in 1952 found Western Insurance Securities trading at roughly 1x earnings ([GuruFocus](https://www.gurufocus.com/news/1149512/some-thoughts-on-warren-buffetts-early-investments-in-western-insurance-services)). In 1951 he put about 65% of his net worth into GEICO and returned about **75.8% against the Dow's 21.3%**. The widely repeated "144%" figure has no source ([GuruFocus](https://www.gurufocus.com/news/248721/how-buffett-crushed-the-dow-in-1951-lessons-for-investing-with-small-sums)). He then apprenticed under Graham at Graham-Newman for $12,000 a year, inside the deal flow of the best value shop in America ([Financial History](https://fhmagazine.org/financial-history-134-summer-2020/0850549001596540706/p15)).

The partnership started in 1956 with **$105,100 from family and friends**. It charged no management fee and took 25% of profits above a 6% hurdle. Limited partners compounded at about **23.8% a year net against 7.4% for the Dow** ([Rational Walk](https://rationalwalk.com/highlights-from-buffett-partnership-letters/)). The trades were concentrated and hands-on. About a quarter of partnership assets went into Sanborn Map, whose investment portfolio was worth more than its share price, and Buffett took a board seat to force the value out ([GuruFocus, 1960 letter](https://www.gurufocus.com/news/7227/warren-buffett-partnership-letter-of-1960)). At Dempster Mill he took 70% control and brought in a turnaround manager ([MOI Global](https://moiglobal.com/warren-buffetts-ground-rules/)). During the 1963 salad-oil scandal he checked whether Omaha restaurants and banks still took American Express, and reportedly built a stake of about 40% of the partnership's assets ([The Grain Desk](https://thegraindesk.substack.com/p/main-street-still-trusted-the-card)). That 40% figure has not been verified against his letters. Buffett himself says small size was the edge: "it's a huge structural advantage not to have a lot of money," and he claimed he could make 50% a year on $1 million ([AOL/Moneywise](https://www.aol.com/finance/warren-buffett-certain-could-earn-121300309.html)).

body: Very large fortunes mostly come from founding or owning a business, not from picking public stocks. "Finance & Investments" produces many billionaires, but they are mostly fund *managers* who collect fees and carry on other people's capital, and dealmakers. They are not retail stock pickers. For every visible winner, there are people who ran the same concentrated or leveraged playbook and were wiped out: Archegos, LTCM, Harshad Mehta and Ketan Parekh, Indian small-cap holders in 2008, and Indian F&O traders.

body:
| Clause | What the auditor must report | Why it matters |
|---|---|---|
| 3(i) | PP&E records, physical verification, title deeds not in company's name, revaluation, **benami** proceedings | Phantom assets |
| 3(ii)(b) | **Quarterly returns/statements filed with banks for working-capital limits vs books**: any material differences | Inflated stock/debtor statements to banks is a fraud precursor |
| 3(iii) | Loans, advances, guarantees to companies, LLPs, firms, **related parties**: terms, overdue amounts, loans repayable on demand | Promoter leakage |
| 3(iv) | Compliance with s.185/186 | Illegal group loans |
| 3(vii) | Undeposited statutory dues (GST, PF, income tax) and disputed dues | Cash stress shows here first |
| 3(viii) | Unrecorded income surrendered in tax assessments | Off-books income |
| 3(ix) | **Defaults on loans**, wilful-defaulter status, short-term funds used for long-term purposes, funds raised to pay subsidiaries' obligations | Covers flag #14 directly |
| 3(x) | Use of IPO/FPO and preferential-allotment money | Diversion |
| 3(xi) | **Fraud** noticed, whistle-blower complaints, s.143(12) reports to Govt | Fraud already occurred |
| 3(xiv) | Internal audit system adequate? | |
| 3(xvi) | NBFC registration / CIC issues | |
| 3(xvii) | **Cash losses** in current and previous year | |
| 3(xviii) | **Resignation of statutory auditors**, and whether outgoing auditor's issues were considered | Flag #9 |
| 3(xix) | **Material uncertainty about meeting liabilities within one year** | India's going-concern lite |
| 3(xxi) | Qualifications/adverse remarks in group companies' CARO reports | Group contagion |

*Tip:* CARO applies to the **standalone** audit report, so read the standalone annual report even when you analyse consolidated numbers. Also read the auditor's **Key Audit Matters**, any **Emphasis of Matter**, the **Internal Financial Controls (IFC) report** (s.143(3)(i)), and **Schedule III "Additional regulatory information"** (CWIP ageing, wilful defaulter, struck-off company dealings, crypto, undisclosed income, and the key ratios with >25% change explanations).

**6. Auditor quality and tenure.** Mandatory rotation applies (s.139: 2 × 5-year terms for audit firms). Watch for mid-term resignation, a small auditor for a large company, and a change from a Big-4/large network to an unknown firm. NFRA orders are public.

- **63-day tests use events whose 63-trading-day window has closed** by the last price date. In practice that means
  Dec-25 and Mar-26, plus most of Jun-26. Events with an open window are excluded from 63d statistics, and the count is
  reported.
- **Sep-2026 quarter: only 21-day results (where that window has closed). Its 63-day result is marked PENDING**
  (closes about mid-Feb 2027). It is not a primary result.
- Quintiles are always assigned among **all** eligible events of the fiscal quarter, whatever their window status. The
  assignment uses only announcement-time information, so it cannot depend on outcomes.

body: US industrial managements **meet or beat their explicit company-level ranges** almost every time: pooled margin delivery is 93% (n=14) and revenue/growth 71% (n=14). Without A. O. Smith, revenue/growth is 100%. The reason is not foresight. These companies **guide conservatively and raise**: Watts raised at every call (FY2026 organic 2–6% → 8–11% → 11–12%), and Lincoln raised its sales guide twice (mid-single digit → high single digit → low teens). The misses sit in three places. (1) **One company's bad year**: A. O. Smith cut its FY2026 guide three times and sold China. Its Jan-2026 items score *withdrawn*. (2) **International and China sub-lines**: A. O. Smith's China was −12% against −5..−8%. (3) **Capex and plant dates**: pooled capacity delivery is 50% credit and 0% strict (n=4). Simpson's capex came in 0.6% over its range, its Gallatin plant was still ramping after its "fully operational by year-end" date, and A. O. Smith's capex was 6% under. That third pattern is the same one seen in India (T&D, auto components). **But the company scores rest on 6–18 scored promises each, and nearly all FY2026 guidance is pending**, so the rule shrinks hard.
